title: A hot thermal echo needs a bright hidden heater for the 2023 ASASSN-14ko UV delay
abstract: We test whether the 2.79-day X-ray-to-UV threshold delay in the 2023 ASASSN-14ko flare can be a pure light-travel echo. Fifteen simultaneous XMM optical monitor UV pairs admit an affine count relation. Full filter response integrals constrain two thermal models. With a 10-percent relative response allowance, a fixed-temperature changing-area model needs at least 2.40e45 erg/s of isotropic heating; a small temperature-change model needs 7.57e44 erg/s. These are 255 and 81 times the measured switching X-ray luminosity. A cold red-leak branch predicts variable optical light at least 178 times the measured total, even with a 30-percent UV response allowance, but that veto uses flagged optical data. The limits assume external thermal balance, heater onset at the X-ray marker, and a fully geometric delay. A hidden extreme-UV heater, internal heating, diffusion, beaming, atmosphere colour corrections and nonthermal spectra can evade them. The UV threshold delay is not a measured transfer-function lag. No orbital stall is proved. We provide code, source hashes, aggregate fits, checks and retrieval instructions.

display.caption: Thermal count ratios and conditional minimum heater power for a fully geometric 2.79-day delay. The optical veto tests the cold branch separately.
